newsitem.title: GERMANY: Graf's father on trial charged with dodging tax.
newsitem.headline: Graf's father on trial charged with dodging tax.

text.p: The father of German tennis star Steffi Graf went on trial on Thursday on charges of illegally diverting millions of marks (dollars) of his daughter's earnings out of the country to avoid taxes.

Peter Graf and family tax adviser Joachim Eckardt face up to 10 years in prison if convicted of depriving tax authorities of 19 million marks ($13 million) -- just under half Steffi Graf's earnings between 1989 and 1993.

Hours earlier the world number one, who is herself still under investigation in the affair, advanced to the semifinals at the U.S. Open in New York but admitted her mind was thousands of miles away in the Mannheim high court.
Her 58-year-old father and advisor, a former used-car salesman, looked calm and relaxed as he was led into the court, near the family home in the southwestern town of Bruehl.
Peter Graf, who was taken into custody in August last year because prosecutors feared he would flee the country, is said to be in poor health.

Graf's lawyer and family friend Kurt Himmelsbach told reporters his defence against a charge sheet running to 237 pages would focus on the way top athletes are taxed, adding: "There are many unresolved problems here."

Steffi Graf is almost alone among Germany's millionaire sports stars in not fleeing to a tax haven abroad, a path well beaten by others such as tennis player Boris Becker and world motor racing champion Michael Schumacher.
Eckardt's lawyers had intended to call the player into the witness stand in the course of the trial.

But her father's lawyer Franz Salditt said he had heard from her attorneys that she would refuse to give evidence to avoid incriminating herself. One of Eckardt's lawyers said this would make it "pointless" to call her into the stand.

Graf, 27, says she handed over her financial affairs to her father from an early age at and took little interest in how much she was earning. Most estimates put her career earnings at over 100 million marks ($67 million).
She has displayed astonishing calm on the court during the affair, winning the U.S. Open last year a month after her father was arrested, and taking two more Grand Slam titles since.
But the media hounding which has accompanied the affair has frequently reduced her to tears off the court.
After her straight-sets quarter-final victory late on Wednesday against Austria's Judith Wiesner, she admitted her mind was elsewhere.
"I guess for some reason it's a little difficult at the moment to focus very well on the court," she said.
"I don't really have the most positive attitude out there. I'll definitely have to work on that."
The trial is expected to last at least four months. ($1=1.4846 Mark)
